title: Why can an unbounded queue be more dangerous than rejecting requests (it converts overload into unbounded latency + memory growth while appearing available), and why does explicit load shedding / bounded queues preserve healthy latency for work the system can actually complete?
shortTitle: Why can an unbounded queue be more dangerous than rejecting requests?
keyPoints: An unbounded queue under sustained overload grows without limit, converting overload into unbounded latency and memory growth.
The system appears available because it keeps accepting requests, but by the time queued work is processed, clients have timed out.
Memory grows as every queued item holds its payload, context, and often a thread, eventually causing GC thrashing or OOM.
A bounded queue caps depth, so maximum latency is also capped: queue size divided by service rate.
Load shedding with 429/503 makes overload a visible, alertable signal instead of a silent collapse.
Intelligent shedding drops the least valuable work first: low-priority, already-timed-out, or cosmetic requests.
In Java, the difference is LinkedBlockingQueue() (unbounded, dangerous) vs LinkedBlockingQueue(capacity) with AbortPolicy.

s1_definition.oneliner: An unbounded queue turns overload into unbounded latency and memory growth while pretending to be healthy; a bounded queue with load shedding keeps accepted work fast and makes overload honest.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Unbounded Queue** – has no capacity limit, so under sustained overload it accepts work faster than it can be processed, growing without bound.
- **Little's Law** – queue depth = arrival rate x time-in-system; if arrivals exceed service rate persistently, depth and latency grow without limit.
- **Silent Failure** – the system appears available (keeps accepting), but queued work ages past usefulness before processing.
- **Bounded Queue** – has a fixed capacity; when full, new work is rejected immediately with a clear signal (429 or 503).
- **Load Shedding** – explicitly rejecting excess work to preserve capacity for the work the system can actually complete.
- **Intelligent Shedding** – drop the least valuable work first: low-priority, already-timed-out, or non-critical path requests.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India one teller processes twenty customers an hour. If the branch lets an unlimited line form, on a busy day a thousand people join. The teller still works, so the branch "looks open," but the person at the back waits fifty hours. The alternative: once the line reaches thirty, the guard says "we are full, please come back later." Everyone in the line is served quickly, and the thirty people get a healthy, predictable wait.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Unbounded Queue Under Overload
  ──────────────────────────────

  Arrivals: 200/s → Queue → Processing: 150/s
                     │
                     │ surplus: 50/s
                     ▼
  Queue depth:  50 → 100 → 150 → 200 → ... → OOM
  Latency:     0.3s → 0.7s → 1.0s → 1.3s → ... → ∞
  Memory:       grows without limit
  Appearance:   "available" (still accepting!)


  Bounded Queue + Load Shedding
  ─────────────────────────────

  Arrivals: 200/s → [Queue cap=100] → Processing: 150/s
                     │
                     │ excess: rejected with 429/503
                     ▼
  Queue depth:  capped at 100
  Latency:     capped at 100/150 = 0.67s
  Memory:       bounded
  Appearance:   honest (shed rate = overload alert)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An unbounded queue looks like a safety feature but under sustained overload it is more dangerous than rejecting work. Little's Law tells the story: if arrivals exceed the service rate persistently, queue depth and latency grow without limit. The system keeps saying "accepted" to every caller, so it looks available, but the queued work ages past usefulness and the system burns capacity on stale requests nobody will read.

A bounded queue with explicit load shedding changes the whole dynamic. When the queue is full, new work is rejected immediately with a 429 or 503. Because depth is capped, maximum latency is also capped. The system does less total work under overload, but all of it is useful. The shed rate becomes a loud, alertable signal instead of a silent slide into collapse.

Intelligent shedding drops the least valuable work first: already-expired requests, non-critical paths, and low-priority operations. In Java the literal difference is `new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()` (unbounded, Integer.MAX_VALUE) versus `new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(100)` with AbortPolicy. Pair server-side shedding with client-side backoff so the system settles into a stable operating point.

Remember one sentence: an unbounded queue does not absorb overload, it stores it as unbounded latency and memory growth, so use a bounded queue with load shedding to keep accepted work fast and make overload honest.
